{"kind":"proof","text":"For each \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Hence the pointwise limit is
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le x<1,\\
1,&x=1.
\end{cases}
\]
Any uniform limit must equal this pointwise limit. Fix \(\varepsilon=\tfrac12\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), choose \(n=N\) and \(x=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x<1\), so \(f(x)=0\), and
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|=x^N=\frac12.
\]
Thus, for every \(N\), there exist \(n\ge N\) and \(x\in[0,1]\) such that \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\ge\varepsilon\). This is the negation of uniform convergence to \(f\). Therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).","reason":""}
